In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of phosphate in groundwater can enhance uranium immobilization in contaminated sediments, but the mechanism of uranium uptake is complex and may be influenced by the geochemistry of the system.
the addition of phosphate to sediments contaminated with U(VI) can enhance U(VI) uptake and immobilization.
the presence of phosphate in the groundwater influent to the columns enhanced U(VI) adsorption to the sediments and reduced the amount of uranium transported through the columns.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the addition of phosphate to a contaminated site could potentially increase the retention of uranium in sediments, but the extent of the increase is dependent on the initial U(VI) concentration in the groundwater.
the addition of phosphate to a contaminated subsurface environment can promote in situ uranium immobilisation, but the rate of uranium uptake is slow.

the presence of phosphate in the synthetic groundwater influents increased U(VI) adsorption onto the sediments and that this effect could be observed for several days after the influent became U(VI)-poor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phosphate addition can be used to promote in situ immobilization of U(VI).
phosphate amendment can promote U(VI) immobilization and retard its transport in contaminated subsurface sediments.
